operations.name: Jorge Rodríguez Mendieta

expected.name: Jorge Rodríguez Mendieta
expected.description:
Jorge Enrique Rodríguez Mendieta, also known as Iván Vargas, commanded the 24th Front of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) and belonged to its Central General Staff. His organizational role is documented in the U.S. prosecution record.

Colombian authorities arrested him in late 2004. He was extradited to the United States on November 1, 2007, and pleaded guilty on December 16, 2009, to conspiring to import cocaine into the United States. On March 19, 2010, U.S. District Judge Thomas F. Hogan sentenced him in Washington, D.C., to 244 months in prison. His plea acknowledged directing cocaine manufacture and distribution with knowledge that some would enter the United States. The conviction concerned that conduct, not simply membership in FARC.

operations.name: Mohammed Rafiq Butt

expected.name: Mohammed Rafiq Butt
expected.description:
Mohammed Rafiq Butt was a 55-year-old Pakistani national held on immigration charges during the detentions following September 11, 2001. He died at Hudson County Correctional Center in New Jersey on October 23, 2001. Human Rights Watch reported that the preliminary autopsy attributed his death to unspecified heart problems and that he had no attorney when he died.

His cellmate told Human Rights Watch that detainees helped Butt submit repeated requests for medical attention during the approximately ten days before his death, without a doctor seeing him in response. The report also noted that he had received antibiotics for a gum infection earlier that month. Human Rights Watch sought an investigation into his death and questioned the adequacy of his care. His case concerns immigration detention and treatment during the national-security dragnet; the sources cited here do not establish that he was prosecuted for personal political activism.

Previous biography:

Mohammed Rafiq Butt was a 55-year-old Pakistani man swept up in the post-September 11 dragnet on September 19, 2001, after a tip that proved baseless — the FBI found no connection between him and the attacks. Cleared of any terrorism suspicion, he was nonetheless kept confined over a visa overstay, and on October 23, 2001 he died of a heart attack in the Hudson County Correctional Center in New Jersey, having seen no lawyer and received no medical attention for his heart condition. He had engaged in no political activity; his case stands as an emblem of the arbitrary, discriminatory national-security detentions that followed September 11.

operations.name: Raphael Joseph

expected.name: Raphael Joseph
expected.description:
Raphael Joseph, also known as Kwesi, was one of the five defendants in the Fountain Valley murder prosecution in the U.S. Virgin Islands. On August 13, 1973, a jury convicted the defendants of first-degree murder, first-degree assault and robbery. In September 1975, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit upheld the denial of their motion for a new trial, which challenged the circumstances of the jury deliberations.

Supporters of the Virgin Island Five describe the defendants as supporters of independence and allege coercion and abuse during the investigation and trial. Those are attributed advocacy claims; the criminal convictions and the appellate ruling remain part of the record. The political-prisoner campaign around the case should be distinguished from a judicial finding that the prosecution was politically motivated.

expected.name: Elizabeth Murray
expected.description:
Elizabeth Murray is an anti-nuclear activist and retired CIA media analyst associated with the Ground Zero Center for Nonviolent Action and the Pacific Life Community.

On March 5, 2025, she and John Heid were arrested for a nonviolent prayer protest on Raytheon property in Tucson, Arizona, opposing nuclear-weapons production. They represented themselves at a September 2 bench trial before Judge Robert Forman in Pima County Consolidated Justice Court. After written guilty verdicts for third-degree criminal trespass, they were sentenced on October 27, 2025, to twenty hours of community service each. Murray described the outcome in the Ground Zero newsletter. The documented sentence was community service, not imprisonment; the available accounts do not establish a multi-day jail stay for this action.

operations.name: Jaan Laaman

expected.name: Jaan Laaman
expected.description:
Jaan Karl Laaman is an anti-imperialist of Estonian heritage who emigrated to the United States as a child. He was a member of the United Freedom Front and was arrested in Cleveland, Ohio in November 1984, shortly after the Levasseurs. He was convicted in 1986 in federal court in Brooklyn of bombing and conspiracy offenses and sentenced to 53 years in federal prison. Separate Massachusetts seditious-conspiracy and racketeering charges were dismissed before trial; they were not convictions. He was also convicted of the 1982 attempted murder of two Massachusetts state troopers in a roadside shootout. He has been held throughout the federal prison system, including the Communications Management Unit at Marion, Illinois. He was released from McCreary Federal Prison on May 15, 2021, as documented by a supporter who accompanied him on release and by the Jericho Movement’s contemporary newsletter. Jaan Laaman was a member of Students for a Democratic Society and is an anti-war and anti-apartheid activist. In 1966, Laaman was first locked up on a non-political robbery charge and his twenty months in prison helped radicalize him. In 1968, Laaman was released and went to Cornell and the University of New Hampshire, where he worked in support of the Black Liberation Movement and the Black Panther Party. In 1979, he and Kazi Toure helped to organize the Amandla Festival of Unity. This concert, which featured Bob Marley, helped to fight racism in Boston and raised money to send to freedom fighters in South Africa. This work led to increased police harassment.

Later, Laaman joined a group known as the United Freedom Front, targeting government institutions and major corporations that had ties to the South African Apartheid system or right-wing paramilitaries in Central America. On February 7, 1982, Laaman and another UFF member, Kazi Toure, were involved in a shoot out with police. While Jaan managed to escape, Kazi was arrested. Despite the arrest, the group continued their operations. However, on November 4, 1984, five members of the group, including Laaman were arrested. Nearly six months later, the last two remaining members were arrested and referred to collectively as the Ohio 7. While originally charged with seditious conspiracy, Laaman was found guilty of five bombings, one attempted bombing, and criminal conspiracy, and was sentenced to 53 years in prison.

In Laaman v. Helgemoe (1977), he was a named plaintiff in a class action over conditions at New Hampshire State Prison. U.S. District Judge Hugh Bownes ordered remedies addressing unconstitutional conditions, including health care, staffing, education and rehabilitation opportunities, visitation and mail. This was a federal district court decision.

Laaman’s release in May 2021 ended the imprisonment that began with his November 1984 arrest.

Previous biography:

Jaan Karl Laaman is an Estonian-born anti-imperialist who emigrated to the United States as a child. He was a member of the United Freedom Front and was arrested in Cleveland, Ohio in November 1984, shortly after the Levasseurs. He was convicted in 1986 in federal court in Brooklyn of seditious conspiracy, racketeering, and bombing in connection with the 1976-84 United Freedom Front actions, and sentenced to 53 years in federal prison. He was also convicted of the 1982 attempted murder of two Massachusetts state troopers in a roadside shootout. He has been held throughout the federal prison system, including the Communications Management Unit at Marion, Illinois. As of 2024 he had served forty years and was the only Ohio 7 defendant other than the deceased still in federal custody. The Jericho Movement lists him among its current political prisoners. Jaan Laaman was a member of Students for a Democratic Society and is an anti-war and anti-apartheid activist. In 1966, Laaman was first locked up on a non-political robbery charge and his twenty months in prison helped radicalize him. In 1968, Laaman was released and went to Cornell and the University of New Hampshire, where he worked in support of the Black Liberation Movement and the Black Panther Party. In 1979, he and Kazi Toure helped to organize the Amandla Festival of Unity. This concert, which featured Bob Marley, helped to fight racism in Boston and raised money to send to freedom fighters in South Africa. This work led to increased police harassment.

Later, Laaman joined a group known as the United Freedom Front, targeting government institutions and major corporations that had ties to the South African Apartheid system or right-wing paramilitaries in Central America. On February 7, 1982, Laaman and another UFF member, Kazi Toure, were involved in a shoot out with police. While Jaan managed to escape, Kazi was arrested. Nearly six months later, the last two remaining members were arrested and referred to collectively as the Ohio 7. In 1977, he won a pivotal case against New Hampshire State Prison, suing after being denied receive reading materials. The New Hampshire Supreme Court, in a decision written by Hugh Bownes, decided in favor of Laaman, and this case eventually was used as a justification for offering college-level education in New Hampshire prisons for the first time.

Laaman was released after serving 37 years.

operations.name: Cliff Cornell

expected.name: Cliff Cornell
expected.description: Specialist Cliff Cornell was a U.S. Army soldier with the 3rd Infantry Division at Fort Stewart, Georgia, who refused deployment to Iraq in early 2005 and fled to Canada. After Canadian authorities denied his refugee claim, he returned voluntarily to the United States in February 2009. Border authorities arrested him on February 4 and held him overnight in Whatcom County Jail before releasing him on February 5 to report to his unit. He subsequently performed regular Army duties while awaiting trial. On April 28, 2009, he pleaded guilty to desertion at Fort Stewart, received a one-year confinement sentence and a bad-conduct discharge, and was jailed. His confinement included the brig at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina. His sentence was reduced by 30 days through clemency, and he was released on January 16, 2010.

He received a five-year sentence under California criminal-syndicalism law and was confined from November 1921 to January 1926. Previous biography (this earlier version combined different people):

George Ryan was an IWW member. George Ryan received a five-year prison sentence, which he served in San Quentin from November 1921 to January 1926. 107 R. J. Sanchez served a prison sentence in San Quentin, where he contracted tuberculosis. He was released in June 1924 on the condition that he would be deported.

George W. Ryan, of Leesburg, Virginia, was a Leesburg citizen held as a hostage for civilians captured by Mosby. He was held as a civilian political prisoner at Fort Delaware during the U.S. Civil War, detained without trial under the wartime suspension of habeas corpus, and is named among the fellow prisoners in the Rev. Isaac W. K. Handy's 1863–1864 prison diary, 'United States Bonds; or, Duress by Federal Authority.'

The June 1925 labor-press political-prisoner birthday notice lists him at San Quentin under prisoner number 35567, with a June 25 birthday (no birth year is given).
